case.why_ai_cites_it: The earliest clear holding that ingesting a corpus wholesale to build an index is transformative. It is the direct ancestor of the argument that training is an indexing-like act rather than a competing publication.

reading.body:
Kelly v. Arriba Soft, a 2003 case holding that a search engine's thumbnail copies of photographs were fair use because they served an indexing function, is cited in defense across the same broad set of AI training lawsuits as Sega v. Accolade.

It is described here as the direct ancestor of the argument that training a model is an indexing-like act rather than a competing publication, which places it early in a lineage of precedents, alongside Sega and HathiTrust elsewhere in this collection, that together form the backbone of the ingestion-is-fair-use defense. Its own stated limit is specific. The original thumbnails were degraded and pointed back to the source material, while a generative system produces new, full-quality output and does not necessarily send anyone back to where it came from, which is exactly the distinction plaintiffs argue breaks the analogy.

The data does not say how courts have ruled on that specific distinction in any of the citing cases, only that the analogy and its stated limit both exist in the record.
